book_title: The Way You Want to Be Loved
subject_line: Assam in The Way You Want to Be Loved
email_body:
Dear Aruni,

I have been following your work from The House with a Thousand Stories through the 2024 collection The Way You Want to Be Loved, and I was struck to read that your Radcliffe project draws on your uncle and grandmother, who worked as traditional healers, or bej, against the violence of 1990s Assam. I would love to ask how family memory and political history share the page in your fiction.

subject_line: Haleema's waiting in The Half Mother
email_body:
Dear Shahnaz,

Haleema in The Half Mother has stayed with me, a woman whose son Imran is taken in the 1990s and who is left not knowing whether he is alive. You have said much of the book was drawn from growing up in the valley, and it later reached French readers as La Mere Orpheline. I would like to ask how teaching literary reportage shapes the way you move between fact and fiction.

subject_line: Loya's journey up the Brahmaputra in Undertow
email_body:
Dear Jahnavi,

In Undertow, Loya travels from Bengaluru to Assam partly to study elephants and partly to find the grandfather, Torun, who watched silently as her mother was cast out. In one interview you said the Brahmaputra runs through Guwahati and so runs through your life too. I would love to ask how that river, and the idea of homecoming you return to since Rebirth, shapes the way you build a family story.

subject_line: The Victorian women botanists behind Everything the Light Touches
email_body:
Dear Janice,

I was intrigued to learn that Everything the Light Touches began with a small exhibition on Victorian women botanists you saw in England, which gave you Evie, and that her story sits alongside Shai's return to Meghalaya and threads of Linnaeus and Goethe. You have also spoken about growing up amid Khasi oral storytelling. I would like to ask how those two inheritances, archive and spoken story, meet in the novel.

subject_line: The darkness that falls in Spirit Nights
email_body:
Dear Easterine,

Spirit Nights stayed with me for its premise: a Naga village plunged into darkness after a taboo is broken, and the people who set out to restore the light. I read that the story grew out of a Naknyulum tale. I would love to ask how you turn an oral tale into a novel without losing the voice it came from.

subject_line: Shenoy Goenbab and the road to The Wait
email_body:
Dear Damodar,

I was moved to read that you once thought of Konkani as only a spoken language, until a book by Shenoy Goenbab changed the course of your life in college. Now The Wait and Other Stories carries your Goan characters to English readers. I would like to ask what you feel is gained, and what is lost, when they cross into English.

subject_line: Twenty-five years in Ranikhet, in Called by the Hills
email_body:
Dear Anuradha,

Called by the Hills, your first book-length non-fiction, follows the life you and Rukun Advani built after moving to Ranikhet some twenty-five years ago. After The Folded Earth, it was striking to read you writing the place directly. I would like to ask how writing the hills as yourself differed from writing them through fictional characters.

book_title: Siddhartha: The Boy Who Became the Buddha
subject_line: Telling Siddhartha's life backwards from enlightenment
email_body:
Dear Advait,

In Siddhartha: The Boy Who Became the Buddha, the story begins at the moment of enlightenment and moves backward through his life. I was also curious to read that you left work as an engine designer to pursue writing and performance before this debut won the 2025 Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar. I would like to ask why you chose to tell the story in reverse.

subject_line: Fathima Island in The Dead Know Nothing
email_body:
Dear Kishore,

The Dead Know Nothing sets its mystery on Fathima Island in the Ashtamudi archipelago, where Thankachan returns home after academic failure just as a body surfaces and a supposedly solved murder case reopens. A review noted its threads of caste, environmental exploitation and brotherly love. I would like to ask how the island itself shaped the plot.

subject_line: The water taps of late-'90s Bangalore in Water Days
email_body:
Dear Sundar,

Water Days caught my attention for its late-'90s Bangalore neighbourhood, where languages mix, water taps double as truth-tellers, and a former security guard becomes an investigator of memory and grief over thirteen days. As a philosopher writing fiction, I would like to ask what the novel lets you think through about language and belonging that an essay could not.
